A lockfile that has not been rebuilt since it was
committed, and a Dockerfile that has not been rebuilt
since it was written, are untested claims. By the end of
this chapter you will be able to look at a green build
and say exactly what it has shown: which of three
automated gates ran, what each one would have caught had
it been absent, and what a missing baseline test still
lets through unnoticed when every gate is green. You will
also know how to turn each gate red on purpose, because a
check that has never been seen to fail has not been shown
to work.

## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 70 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-testing supplies
`tinytest`, the four kinds of test, and the baseline test
this chapter's verification gate runs. Chapter 3
(@sec-levels) supplies the L0-L3 ladder and the
capture-versus-validation vocabulary this chapter makes
operational. Chapter 6 (@sec-dependencies) supplies the
dependency invariant the dependency-manifest gate
automates, and Chapter 7 (@sec-containers) supplies the
Dockerfile the verify job rebuilds. The R knowledge
assumed is writing and calling a function. No prior YAML
is assumed. The chapter's first workflow is a short file
that is read construct by construct, and the shell
primer's [Reading YAML](shell-primer.qmd#sec-shell-yaml)
section covers the syntax.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- explain why a CI runner, carrying none of the author's
  undeclared state, catches a 'works on my machine'
  failure that no test run on the author's own machine
  can?
- name the three automated gates a CI workflow runs,
  state what each one proves, and demonstrate how to make
  each one fail on purpose?
- say why verification (L3) compares computational
  outputs against a committed baseline, within a stated
  tolerance, rather than comparing rendered PDFs or HTML?
- read and extend a checksum manifest that guards the
  integrity of raw input data?
- match the three gates, plus verification, to a
  compendium's archetype, so that a package, a
  manuscript, and a simulation each run only the checks
  appropriate to them?

**Outline.** We begin with where CI sits on the stack, a
captured environment that nobody has yet rebuilt, and the
analyst's three irreplaceable judgments. We then turn to
the machine that is not yours, to a first workflow that
runs the tests on every push, to the three gates and
where their bugs hide, to secrets, tokens, and pinned
actions, and to other forges. The middle of the chapter
treats verification and level L3, the checksum manifest,
and how CI adapts to five archetypes. We then
consider independent external verification, a worked
example, debugging a failed reproduction, and a gate
demonstrated on this book's own cohort compendium.
Lastly, we discuss collaborating with an LLM, followed by
exercises, a cheat sheet, and further reading.

## Check your understanding: from earlier chapters

Two colleagues rerun a compendium in the same
digest-pinned image, built from a complete lockfile.
Colleague A mounts the project without its `.Rprofile`,
where the author had put
`RNGkind(sample.kind = 'Rounding')` and `set.seed(2024)`,
and the bootstrap interval moves. Colleague B, on a
different processor, obtains regression coefficients that
agree with the author's except in their last few digits. For each
discrepancy, name the determinant layer behind it, say
whether any rung of the ladder closes it, and give the
earlier remedy.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Of the two discrepancies in this warm-up, colleague A's
lies in session configuration. The R release fixes the
default sampler at L2, but the `.Rprofile` overrode it,
and an override is fixed only by an explicit `RNGkind()`
call in the analysis code (@sec-levels). The seed belongs
there too, set at the call that draws the resamples, not
in `.Rprofile` (@sec-testing). Colleague B's lies in the
numerical libraries, the BLAS and LAPACK beneath
`crossprod()` and `solve()`. No rung guarantees that
layer: an image determines which BLAS is installed, but
the thread count and the processor still vary
(@sec-levels). The remedy is a baseline test that
compares at a stated tolerance, wide enough to absorb
reordered floating-point sums and too narrow for a
changed coefficient to pass (@sec-testing).
:::
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

Continuous integration pins nothing, and @fig-stack-ci
marks that explicitly. The three layers its gates touch
(package versions, analysis code, and input data) are
validated here, not captured, because the lockfile, the
scripts, and the raw extract were already pinned or
written by the chapters that came before. This chapter's
whole contribution is confirming, on a machine that is
not the author's, that those captures still hold.

## Orientation

Consider a registry study whose analysis is finished,
whose manuscript is written, and whose lockfile and
container recipe are committed to version control. The
author has done, to all appearances, everything this
book has asked. The packages are pinned (@sec-dependencies),
the environment is fixed in an image (@sec-containers),
the report is literate and regenerates its own figures
(@sec-literate). The compendium sits, by the author's
account, at level L2, a pinned environment. But how
does the author know that the captured environment
actually rebuilds, on a machine that is not the one
where the work was done? Until something tests it, the
author does not know.
A lockfile can reference a package version that has
been pulled from its repository. A Dockerfile can
depend on a base image whose digest has drifted. A
script can silently rely on a file that lives only in
the author's home directory and was never committed.
None of these announce themselves on the machine where
the work already runs, because on that machine the
missing piece is present.

In this chapter we take up the instrument that closes
the gap between a reproducibility claim and its
demonstration. Continuous integration, abbreviated CI,
is a service that rebuilds the
compendium from its committed inputs on every change.
It works in a fresh environment that carries none of
the developer's accumulated and undeclared state, and
runs a battery of checks against the result.

We then take the ladder to its top rung. Verification,
the L2-to-L3 transition, confirms what has been captured
by regenerating the computational outputs. It compares
them, number for number and within a stated tolerance,
against a recorded baseline. The subtlety, which we
shall press, is in what gets compared. We compare a
derived dataset, a fitted model object, or a results
table, and emphatically not the rendered PDF or HTML,
whose bytes carry timestamps and font identifiers that
defeat a naive comparison. We close with the schemes by
which reproducibility is checked from outside the
author's own project entirely, during peer review.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what CI does not know

An author claims their compendium is at level L2 because
a `Dockerfile` is committed and builds on their laptop.
Does a green CI run of that same `Dockerfile` raise the
compendium's level? What, precisely, does the green run
add?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The level is set by what is captured, not by who
rebuilds it (@fig-stack-ci). Whether the
compendium is at L2 at all depends on what else is
committed: the rungs are cumulative, so a `Dockerfile`
reaches L2 only beside a lockfile, and without one the
compendium is at L0. The green CI run adds assurance
rather than capture: it shows that the same `Dockerfile`
also builds on a machine that carries none of the
author's undeclared state, which the laptop build alone
cannot show. A build that only ever succeeds on the author's own
machine is exactly the 'works on my machine' pattern this
chapter opened with.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Before turning to the machinery, we note what it cannot
do. Continuous integration is highly automated, but
copying a workflow file into a repository and forgetting
it leaves three decisions unmade. They remain the
analyst's, and no tool makes them.

1. **The analyst decides what counts as a correct
   output, and records the baseline.** Verification can
   compare a regenerated result against a recorded one,
   but it cannot know which results matter or what
   tolerance is acceptable. The baseline may be a
   derived dataset, a coefficient table, or a single
   summary statistic. The agreement required may be to
   the last bit or to a stated numerical tolerance. Both
   are scientific choices the analyst must make and
   defend.

2. **The analyst decides which gates the compendium's
   archetype warrants.** A CI workflow can run `R CMD
   check`, a render gate, and a dependency-manifest gate,
   but not every archetype needs all three. An R-package
   archetype has no report to render; a simulation
   archetype may run a reduced pipeline under CI and the
   full one elsewhere. Matching the gates to the
   archetype is the analyst's call. The aim is that CI
   tests what actually needs testing, without imposing a
   render gate on a project that has nothing to render.

3. **The analyst reads a CI failure as evidence.** A red
   build is CI doing its job: it has found, on a clean
   machine, a dependency the author's machine supplied
   silently. The discipline is to treat the failure as a
   true report about the compendium's reproducibility and
   to fix the captured inputs rather than the check.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Continuous integration (CI).** A hosted service that,
  on every committed change to a repository, checks out
  the code onto a fresh virtual machine, rebuilds the
  project, and runs a defined set of checks, reporting
  success or failure automatically.
- **Workflow.** The file, written in YAML, that tells the
  CI service what to do: which events trigger it, what
  environment to run in, and what commands to execute. On
  GitHub these files live under `.github/workflows/`; on
  GitLab the single file is `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- **Runner.** The fresh, ephemeral machine (usually a
  virtual machine or a container) on which the CI service
  executes the workflow. It is discarded after the run,
  so nothing persists between runs except what the
  workflow explicitly restores.
- **`R CMD check`.** R's own quality gate for a package,
  which among many checks verifies that every dependency
  declared in `DESCRIPTION` is installed and findable. A
  research compendium built as an R package inherits this
  gate for free, for its package skin only: `analysis/`
  is excluded from the build and never checked.
- **Render gate.** A CI check that re-renders the
  compendium's report (an R Markdown or Quarto document)
  from source and fails the build if the render errors.
- **Dependency-manifest gate.** A CI check that enforces
  the dependency invariant of @sec-dependencies. In its
  strict, R-package form it requires every package the code
  uses to be declared in `DESCRIPTION` and pinned in
  `renv.lock`. A research compendium's `DESCRIPTION`
  declares only the API exported from `R/`, while its
  analysis scripts legitimately draw on packages present
  in `renv.lock` but not in `DESCRIPTION`. For a
  compendium, therefore, the gate enforces the weaker
  inclusion that every package the code uses is pinned in
  `renv.lock`.
- **Verification.** The act of rebuilding the compendium's
  environment from its recipe and re-running the analysis
  in it. The regenerated computational outputs are then
  compared with a committed baseline, within a stated
  tolerance, by means of a baseline test (@sec-testing);
  passing it is what the ladder calls level L3.
- **Checksum.** A short fingerprint, computed from a
  file's or an object's bytes by a hash function such as
  SHA-256, with the property that any change to the input,
  however small, changes the fingerprint. A stored
  checksum lets a later run detect that an input has been
  altered.
- **Forge.** The platform that hosts the repository and
  runs its CI, such as GitHub or GitLab. The forge governs
  where the code lives and which CI dialect the workflow
  is written in; it pins nothing about the computational
  environment.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the analyst's irreplaceable judgments

Name the one of the three analyst judgments that a
workflow file, however carefully written, cannot make for
itself, and say why.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Any of the three qualifies, but the clearest is the
first: deciding what counts as a correct output and
recording the baseline. A workflow can run a comparison
and report its result. However, it has no way to decide
which quantity matters, which outputs to compare, or what
tolerance distinguishes a real change from floating-point
noise. That is a scientific judgment about the analysis,
and the CI configuration cannot make it.
:::
:::

## The machine that is not yours

We begin with the reason a second machine is needed at
all. An analysis reproduces on the machine where it was
written partly because the machine is generous. It
supplies, without being asked, a package installed
months ago and never recorded, or a system library that
some other project needed. It may equally supply a data
file sitting in a home directory, or an environment
variable set once in a shell profile. Every one of these
is undeclared state, and every one of them is invisible
precisely because it is present. The 'works on my machine' report is true: it
describes a machine that happens to carry more than the
compendium declares.

Continuous integration removes the generosity. When a
change is pushed, the CI service provisions a fresh
runner, a virtual machine or container that has just
been created and carries nothing but a clean operating
system. It checks out exactly what is under version
control, no more, and attempts to rebuild the
compendium from those committed inputs alone. If the
analysis depended on anything the author never declared,
the rebuild fails. It fails here, rather than in a
reviewer's hands or a colleague's re-analysis a year on.
The CI machine catches the 'works on my machine' failure
at its source for a reason that is almost tautological:
the CI machine is, by construction, not the author's. It
cannot supply the author's undeclared state because it
does not have it.

What CI adds is a repeated, adversarial test. A
compendium that is captured but never retested suffers a
slow decay: its declared environment silently stops
rebuilding as its external references drift, and no one
notices because no one has tried to rebuild it. CI is the
standing test that would notice.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why the runner is generous nowhere

Explain, in one or two sentences, why a freshly
provisioned CI runner cannot supply the undeclared state
that makes an analysis 'work on my machine', and why this
is close to a tautology rather than a clever design
feature.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The runner cannot supply undeclared state because it has
none to supply: it was created moments ago from a clean
image and has never run anything else. It is almost a
tautology because the property that makes it useful,
carrying nothing of the author's, is simply what 'fresh'
means. No engineering insight is required to make a
runner forget what it never knew.
:::
:::

## Your first workflow {#sec-ci-first-workflow}

Before the three gates, we set up the smallest workflow
that is still useful. It restores the lockfile on a fresh
runner and runs the test suite, and nothing more. It
assumes a compendium structured as an R package
(@sec-compendium). It also assumes that `renv.lock`, the
`.Rprofile` that `renv` writes, and `renv/activate.R` are
committed, and that `tinytest` and `pkgload` are recorded
in the lockfile.

A workflow is a text file in the repository. GitHub runs
the files it finds in the directory `.github/workflows/`,
and each must end in `.yml` or `.yaml`
[@githubworkflowsyntax]. We save the following as
`.github/workflows/tests.yml`:

```yaml
name: tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: renv
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - name: Run the tests
        run: |
          Rscript --version
          Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

Read from the top, the file names the workflow `tests` and
runs it on every push to the branch `main`. A repository
whose default branch is still called `master` must say so
here, or the workflow never starts. The token the job
receives may read the repository's contents and is
granted nothing more (@sec-ci-secrets). The one job,
also called `tests`, runs on a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu
runner, and its four steps run in order. The first
copies the repository onto the runner. The second
installs the R version recorded in `renv.lock`,
which is not necessarily the newest release;
`r-version: renv` is what requests it. The third installs
`renv` and restores every package in the lockfile into
the project library. The fourth prints the R version, for
the record, and runs the test script. The actions are
pinned by major-version tag, as elsewhere in this
chapter; @sec-ci-secrets explains why a commit SHA is
safer. @tbl-ci-reading-workflow reads the six constructs
the file uses.

| Construct | In the file | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Key and value | `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` | A name, a colon, a space, and a value. The space after the colon is required. |
| List item | `- uses: actions/checkout@v7` | A dash and a space begin one item of a list. `steps` is such a list, run from top to bottom; `[main]` is a list written on one line. |
| Nesting | `push:` indented under `on:` | Indentation places a key inside the one above it. Keys at the same level must start in the same column, and YAML forbids tabs for indentation. |
| Expression | `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` | Not YAML: to YAML it is plain text. GitHub evaluates it rather than treating it as a string, here inserting a token issued for the run. |
| Block scalar | `run: |` | The indented lines that follow form one text value, with their line breaks kept. GitHub runs them in one shell, and the default shell stops at the first failing line. |
| Quoting | `r-version: '4.10'` | An unquoted value that looks like a number is read as one, so `4.10` becomes 4.1. Quotes keep the value as text. |

: Reading the workflow. Each row names a YAML or GitHub Actions construct, quotes an example from `tests.yml` (the last row's example is not in the file), and states how it is read [@githubworkflowsyntax; @githubexpressions]. {#tbl-ci-reading-workflow}

The test script is the first form of a file that
@sec-verification-l3 extends with a baseline check. It
exists because the one-line call
`tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')` exits with
status 0 even when a test fails. A runner judges a step
only by its exit status, so that call would always show
success. The script converts a failure into status 1:

```r
# ci/run-tests.R
pkgload::load_all('.', quiet = TRUE)
res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')
print(res)
if (!tinytest::all_pass(res)) quit(status = 1)
```

We ran it on a toy package with one passing test and one
deliberately failing test. The bare call exited with 0,
and the script exited with 1.

Committing the two files and pushing them to `main` is the
event that starts the run [@githubquickstart]. The result
appears in two places. The repository's Actions tab lists
every run of every workflow. Clicking a run, and then its
job, shows each step in turn, and a failed step is
expanded automatically to show its log [@githubrunlogs].
The commit itself also carries the run's status, passed
or failed, shown beside it in the commit list and on any
pull request it belongs to [@githubstatuschecks].

This book's house rule, that a gate is not shown to work
until it has been seen to fail, applies to the first
workflow too. The habit has five steps. We push the
workflow and confirm that the run passes. We then add a
`library()` call for a package that is not in the
lockfile, such as `library(fixest)`, to a test file, and
push again. The runner has only what `renv.lock` declares,
so the run fails. We open the failed step and read the
line that names the cause. On our toy package, outside a
runner, the same script printed it as

```
Error in library(fixest) : there is no package called 'fixest'
```

and exited with status 1. Lastly, we remove the call, or
install the package and record it with `renv::snapshot()`,
and push once more to see the run pass. A workflow that
has never been seen to fail has not been shown to check
anything.

The commonest first failure is not in R at all. YAML reads
structure from indentation, so a line moved by a few
spaces changes, or breaks, the file. We moved
`r-version: renv` three columns to the left of where it
belongs, under `with:`, and parsed the result with R's
`yaml::yaml.load()`:

```
Parser error: while parsing a block collection at line
16, column 7 did not find expected '-' indicator at line
19, column 8
```

The message is wrapped here to fit the page. The parser
was reading the `steps` list, which begins at line 16,
column 7. At line 19 it met a line that was neither a new
item nor part of the previous one. GitHub cannot run such
a file either. We did not push one, so GitHub's own
message is not reproduced here. Running
`yaml::read_yaml('.github/workflows/tests.yml')` locally,
or opening the file in an editor that marks YAML errors,
catches the mistake before the push. Such a check
confirms only the syntax. A key that is misspelled but
correctly indented parses without complaint and is
rejected, if at all, by GitHub. The shell primer's
[Reading YAML](shell-primer.qmd#sec-shell-yaml) section covers the syntax
in more detail.

## What the checks are: the three gates

A CI run on a research compendium executes, in the
general case, three gates. We take them in turn, because
the division of labor among them is exact.

The first is **`R CMD check`**. Because a research
compendium is structured as an R package (@sec-compendium),
it inherits R's own quality gate at no additional cost.
Among its many checks, the one that matters most for
reproducibility is early and simple. It verifies that
every package the code in `R/` uses is declared in
`DESCRIPTION`, and that every declared package is
installed and findable. On a fresh runner this is a real
test, because the runner has only what the lockfile
declared.

Its scope is narrower than it looks. The
check runs on the package that `R CMD build` makes, and a
compendium's `.Rbuildignore` excludes `analysis/`. The
analysis scripts are therefore never parsed, never run,
and never scanned for packages (@sec-compendium).
`R CMD check` validates the package skin, `R/`, the
tests, and `DESCRIPTION`, and nothing else. Within that
scope there is a second trap. An undeclared package used
in `R/` is reported as a WARNING, not an ERROR, so the
gate fails on it only if it is told to fail on warnings.
A workflow that passes `error_on = 'error'` to
`rcmdcheck`, as many hand-written workflows do, lets the
undeclared dependency through with a green build.

The second is the **render gate**. Where the compendium
carries a report, an R Markdown or Quarto document that
regenerates its own figures and tables, the workflow
re-renders it from source on the runner. A render that
errors, because a chunk references an object that no
longer exists or a package that was not restored, fails
the build. Of the three gates it is the one that executes
the analysis code: a report that sources the
scripts under `analysis/`, or calls the functions they
define, runs them on the runner, against the restored
library and nothing else. The render gate is the literate
document's validation counterpart: @sec-literate seals
the prose to the code, and the render gate confirms, on a
clean machine, that the seal holds. It needs the data on
the runner. The cohort this book uses is synthetic and
committed for that reason. Where the real data are
restricted, CI renders against a synthetic stand-in, and
the real render runs inside the environment approved for
the data. Committing the data to turn a red render gate
green is never the fix.

The third is the **dependency-manifest gate**, the
automated form of the dependency invariant developed in
@sec-dependencies. In its strict form, appropriate to the
R-package archetype, the invariant is a double inclusion.
The set of packages the code actually uses must be a
subset of the set declared in `DESCRIPTION`, which must in
turn be a subset of the set pinned in `renv.lock`. A
research compendium is looser. Its `DESCRIPTION` declares
only the API exported from `R/`, while its analysis
scripts legitimately use packages that appear in
`renv.lock` but never in `DESCRIPTION`. For a compendium
the operative invariant is therefore the single inclusion
that every package the code uses is pinned in `renv.lock`,
and the strict `DESCRIPTION`-inclusion gate does not apply.
The gate scans the source for `library()`, `require()`,
and `pkg::fun()` calls. It then reads `renv.lock`, and
`DESCRIPTION` in the strict form, and stops with an error
if a used package is not pinned. Because it reads the analysis scripts, it is
the gate that covers what `R CMD check` cannot see. Its
core needs no special tool; `renv` itself can find the
packages the code uses. The minimal version below scans
only `analysis/`, the part `R CMD check` never reads:

```r
# ci/dependency-gate.R
used <- unique(renv::dependencies('analysis')$Package)
locked <- names(renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')$Packages)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))
missing <- setdiff(used, c(locked, base_pkgs))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  stop('Used in analysis/ but not pinned in renv.lock: ',
       toString(missing))
}
```

Run as `Rscript ci/dependency-gate.R` from the repository
root, the script's `stop()` ends R with a nonzero exit
status, which is what fails the step. It catches the most
common drift: a package installed interactively during
analysis, used in the code, and never snapshotted, so
that the lockfile is silently incomplete. We ran it on a
toy project whose lockfile pinned `digest` and `renv`.
With a script in `analysis/` that loaded `digest`, it
exited with status 0. After `library(sandwich)` was added
to that script, it printed

```
Finding R package dependencies ... Done!
Error: Used in analysis/ but not pinned in renv.lock: sandwich
Execution halted
```

and exited with status 1.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## With zzcollab

The companion package `zzrenvcheck` does the same scan
with more care: tests, vignettes, version constraints,
and the stricter `DESCRIPTION` inclusion for the package
archetype. A gate step would call
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE, error_on_fail = TRUE)`.
Passing `error_on_fail = TRUE` explicitly keeps the
step's failure from depending on how R was started. The
package is not on CRAN, so a workflow installs it with
`remotes::install_github('rgt47/zzrenvcheck', ref = <commit>)`,
pinned to a commit. In a scaffolded project,
`make check-renv-no-fix` runs this check without
modifying anything. The similarly named `make check-renv`
repairs `renv.lock` in place and is therefore not a gate.
:::

How do the three gates fit together in practice? A
condensed GitHub Actions workflow that runs them on every
push and pull request illustrates the shape of the
thing. It uses the R community's `r-lib/actions` for the
setup and the check, at the major versions current when
this chapter was revised in November 2026
(`actions/checkout@v7`, `r-lib/actions/*@v2`). We show
it as a static file. Its
YAML was checked for syntax, and the command in each gate
was run against a toy compendium. However, the workflow
as a whole is executed by the CI service, never by this
book.

```yaml
name: compendium

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  gates:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Install the R version recorded in renv.lock.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: renv
          use-public-rspm: true

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-pandoc@v2

      # Restore renv.lock into the project library. A
      # stock renv .Rprofile activates that library in
      # every later R step run from the repository root.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2

      # The check tool is not an analysis dependency, so
      # it is not in renv.lock.
      - name: Install the gate tools
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          renv::install('rcmdcheck')

      # Gate 1: R CMD check of the package skin. Any
      # WARNING, such as an undeclared import, fails.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          args: 'c("--no-manual")'
          error-on: '"warning"'

      # Gate 2: every package used in analysis/ is
      # pinned in renv.lock.
      - name: Dependency-manifest gate
        run: Rscript ci/dependency-gate.R

      # Gate 3: the report re-renders from source.
      - name: Render gate
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          rmarkdown::render('analysis/report/report.Rmd',
                            output_format = 'html_document',
                            output_dir = tempdir())
```

Three choices in the file merit a word. First, `error-on`
is set to `"warning"` explicitly, although that is also
the action's default. The setting is the whole difference
between a gate that catches an undeclared import and one
that does not. Second, the render gate renders to HTML
into a temporary folder. It tests that every chunk runs,
and leaves PDF typesetting, which needs a LaTeX
installation, to a separate step if the deliverable is a
PDF. Third, nothing in the file is marked
`continue-on-error`; a step that is allowed to fail
without failing the job is a report, not a gate.

The house rule of this book is that a gate is not shown to
work until it has been seen to fail. Each of the three can
be turned red on purpose, in a branch, in a few minutes:

| Gate | Deliberate breakage | What the run reports |
|---|---|---|
| `R CMD check` | Call `sandwich::vcovHC()` in a function in `R/` without adding `sandwich` to `DESCRIPTION` | A WARNING, '`::` or `:::` import not declared from', which `error-on: '"warning"'` turns into a failed step |
| Dependency manifest | Add `library(sandwich)` to a script in `analysis/` without snapshotting | The missing package is listed and the step stops with an error |
| Render | Add a chunk that loads a package absent from `renv.lock`, or uses an object no chunk creates | `rmarkdown::render()` stops at that chunk and names it |

We ran the first and third breakages against a toy
compendium (R 4.6.1, `rcmdcheck` 1.4.0) in October 2026,
and the second against the toy project above (R 4.6.2,
`renv` 1.3.1) in November 2026. Each command exited with
a nonzero status. The first breakage also shows why the
setting matters: with `error_on = 'error'` the same check
returned normally, the WARNING printed and ignored.
Placing `library(sandwich)` in `analysis/` instead of
`R/` shows the scope of the first gate. In that case
`R CMD check` passes and the dependency gate goes red;
the render gate goes red too if the report runs that
script.

### Where CI bugs hide: cross-boundary state

The workflow above takes care over where the pinned
library is restored and from which directory each R step
starts. That care avoids a subtle bug whose cause
generalizes well beyond the particular case.

The trouble is that a CI run is not one continuous
process. It is a sequence of separate steps, each a fresh
shell, and within a step the check itself runs in a
further separate subprocess. State does not automatically
cross these boundaries. In one documented case, the step
that restored the pinned packages installed them
correctly. The very next step, running `R CMD check`,
then reported a required package as 'not available'. The
package was on disk; the check simply could not see where.
Two boundaries conspired. The restore step adjusted the
library path in its own shell, but the next step is a
fresh shell and inherited none of that. And even within
a step, `R CMD check` runs in a child subprocess whose
library path must be passed to it explicitly. Adjusting
the path in the calling session does not propagate to the
child. The fix is to launch the check from a session in
which the restored library is already on the library
path, and to make sure that path travels to the child.

In the workflow above, three pieces combine to do this.
`setup-renv` restores into the project library. Every
later R step starts in the repository root, where the
project's `.Rprofile` activates that library. And
`rcmdcheck()` hands the calling session's `.libPaths()`
to the check subprocess, which is the default of its
`libpath` argument. A workflow that restores into some
other folder must pass that folder to `libpath` by hand.

The second piece is an assumption, and it is the same
cross-boundary bug in waiting. It holds for the stock
`.Rprofile` that `renv::init()` writes, which sources
`renv/activate.R` in every session. It does not hold for
a customized `.Rprofile` that activates renv only under
some condition, such as running inside a container. On a
CI host such a profile skips renv, and later steps see
the system library rather than the restored one. Such a
compendium must activate the library explicitly on the
runner, for example by beginning each R step with
`source('renv/activate.R')`.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## With zzcollab

The `.Rprofile` that `zzcollab` scaffolds is of this
conditional kind: it activates renv only when the
environment variable `ZZCOLLAB_CONTAINER` is set to
`true`, as the scaffolded `Dockerfile` sets it. On a CI
host, set that variable in the job's `env:` block, or
source `renv/activate.R` as above.
:::

But why did the bug stay hidden? The workflow had passed
for several repositories, because each of them imported
only packages that the generic container base image
already provided; the restored library was never
actually needed. The defect surfaced only when a
repository imported a specialized modeling package absent
from the base image. The broader literature on why
deposited analyses fail to re-run [@trisovic2022]
documents how often re-execution simply fails. The
particular fault here is cross-boundary state, the state
that must pass from one step, shell, or process to the
next and silently does not. It is where CI bugs hide. A
dormant defect of this kind needs an adversarial input,
a dependency outside the comfortable base image, to bring
it to light. A check that passes tells us only that
nothing has yet exercised it hard enough to fail.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: a package that is there and not there

A workflow restores the lockfile in one step. In the next
step, `R CMD check` reports a pinned package as 'not
available', although the package is on disk. Name the two
boundaries the library path failed to cross.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The first is the boundary between steps: each step is a
fresh shell, so a library path set in the restore step's
shell is gone in the next. The second is the boundary
between the calling R session and the check subprocess,
which sees only the library path it is handed. The fix
is a session whose library path already includes the
restored library, passed on to the check.
:::
:::

## Secrets, tokens, and pinned actions {#sec-ci-secrets}

Before going further with verification, we pause on a
matter of hygiene. A CI runner holds credentials the
author's own laptop never needed, to comment on a pull
request, push a built image, or deploy a rendered report.
A leaked credential is a worse incident than a failed
reproducibility check. It warrants the same discipline
this chapter applies elsewhere: nothing should reach the
runner, or leave it, undeclared.

The first rule is never to let a secret reach a log or a
commit. GitHub's guidance on securing Actions workflows warns
that sensitive values 'should never be stored as plaintext in
workflow files' [@githubhardening]. A workflow instead
references a stored secret through the `secrets` context,
`${{ secrets.NAME }}`. The runner substitutes the value at
execution time, and GitHub attempts to redact it from the
log. The redaction is best effort: 'automatic redaction is
not guaranteed', and the documentation recommends auditing
how a workflow handles secrets to confirm one is never
explicitly printed [@githubhardening]. The condensed
workflow earlier in this chapter already follows the
pattern. Its line
`GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` passes a credential
into the job's environment without ever writing its value
into the file.

The second rule is least privilege. The default permissions of
the token GitHub Actions issues a job come from a repository,
organization, or enterprise setting, which may be permissive.
A workflow with no `permissions` block inherits that setting
and can run with more access than most jobs need. GitHub's
hardening guidance calls
a default of read-only repository contents 'good security
practice', with individual jobs granted more only where they
need it [@githubhardening]. The chapter's own example
already does this: it declares `permissions: contents: read`
at the top of the workflow.

The third rule has a direct parallel already established in
this book. @sec-containers showed that pinning a base image
by tag is not enough. A tag is a mutable pointer that a
maintainer can repoint to different bytes with no change to
the Dockerfile that names it; pinning by digest is what
actually fixes the bytes a build receives. A third-party
GitHub Action carries the same hazard. A
version tag such as `@v7` can be moved to a different commit
by its maintainer, or by anyone who compromises the
maintainer's account. The workflow that trusts the tag then
runs whatever that commit contains on its next trigger, with
no diff in the consuming repository to review. GitHub's own
hardening guidance recommends pinning a third-party action to
a full-length commit SHA rather than a tag. It states the
rationale plainly: a tag 'can be moved or deleted' by anyone
with write access to the action's repository, while forging a
given commit SHA would need an attacker to produce a SHA-1
collision [@githubhardening]:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
```

The trailing comment records which release the SHA was
taken from, since forty hex characters say nothing to a
human reader. A SHA pin does not move on its own, so it
also does not pick up a security fix. Dependabot or
Renovate can watch the pinned actions and open a pull
request that replaces the SHA and its comment when a new
release appears, so that each update is a reviewed
commit rather than a silent change.

The chapter's own workflow examples fall short of their
own advice. They should be read as a teaching
simplification, not a model to copy unchanged. The
actions above (`actions/checkout@v7` and
`r-lib/actions/*@v2`) pin by tag, and `rcmdcheck` is
installed at whatever version is current. This book's
Dockerfile
explains a recipe by tag before showing the digest-pinned
version, and for the same reason: a tag is legible in a
worked example in a way forty hex characters are not.
A compendium's actual CI configuration should pin every
third-party action to a commit SHA, exactly as its
Dockerfile pins its base image by digest. A dependency
that can change with no commit to the project's own
history is undeclared state, whether it lives in a
package repository, a container registry, or an action's git
history.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what a version tag on an action actually promises

A teammate argues that pinning an action with `uses:
some-org/some-action@v3` is already safe, since the tag is
version-controlled and anyone can see which commit `v3` points
to on GitHub. What is wrong with this argument?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Visible is not the same as fixed. A tag is a label the
action's maintainer, or anyone with write access to that
repository, can repoint to a different commit at any time.
The workflow records only the label it asked for, not which
commit it ran last time. Checking what `v3` resolves to now
answers only 'what would run if I checked right now'. It
does not answer what ran last week, or what will run if the
tag moves before the next trigger. A commit SHA fixes the
content; a tag, however carefully maintained, is a pointer
that can be moved. This is exactly the distinction this
book already draws between a Docker tag and a Docker
digest.
:::
:::

## Other forges

The forge that hosts a repository is often not the
researcher's choice. Many universities run their own
GitLab, whose CI expresses the same gates in a different
dialect, a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` of stages and scripts.
A workflow written once per dialect is a workflow
maintained twice. The remedy is to single-source
the checking logic in the project's own `Makefile`, one
target per gate. Each forge's CI file then shrinks to a
thin shim that checks out the code and calls `make`, and
the same commands run on the analyst's machine.
@sec-ci-other-forges gives the GitLab translation of this
chapter's workflow and discusses workflows that configure
themselves from the files a repository contains.

## Verification and level L3 {#sec-verification-l3}

The first three gates confirm that the compendium builds,
checks, and renders on a clean machine. They do not
confirm that it produces the *same numbers*. That is the
work of verification, the L2-to-L3 transition and the top
of the ladder, which confirms what has been captured.

L3, as @sec-levels defines it, requires that recorded
outputs be shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance
from a clean rebuild. Each part of that sentence names a
mechanism. The recorded outputs and the tolerance live in
a *baseline test* (@sec-testing): a committed
file of key estimates is recorded once, and a test file
named `test-baseline-*.R` recomputes them and compares
with `expect_equal(..., tolerance = ...)`. The clean
rebuild is the project's own image, built from its
`Dockerfile` on a machine that has never seen it.
Verification is running the first inside the second, and
it fails if either fails. It fails if the image does not
rebuild, if any test fails, or if no baseline test runs
at all. A test suite without a baseline test can pass in
a rebuilt image and show that the environment is sound,
which is L2 confirmed. However, it has compared nothing
with a recorded result, so it is not L3.

In continuous integration this is a second job in the same
workflow, run after the gates pass:

```yaml
  verify:
    needs: gates
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # L2: the project's own Dockerfile must rebuild.
      - name: Rebuild the project image
        run: docker build -t compendium:ci .

      # L3: the test suite, with at least one baseline
      # test, must pass inside the rebuilt image.
      - name: Run the tests in the image
        run: >
          docker run --rm
          -e RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE
          -v "$PWD":/work -w /work
          compendium:ci Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

The test step runs `ci/run-tests.R`, the script of
@sec-ci-first-workflow, which already turns a failed
expectation into a nonzero exit. For L3 it gains one
check. It refuses to pass if no baseline test produced a
result, which is the case when the baseline file is
missing or when its guard found no data and exited early:

```r
# ci/run-tests.R
pkgload::load_all('.', quiet = TRUE)
res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')
print(res)
ran <- unique(as.data.frame(res)$file)
if (!any(grepl('^test-baseline', ran))) {
  stop('No baseline test ran, so this is not an L3 check.')
}
if (!tinytest::all_pass(res)) quit(status = 1)
```

Two assumptions are built in and should be checked
against the image in use. The image must contain
`tinytest` and `pkgload`, which means they must be in the
lockfile it restores. And because
`RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE` stops the mounted
project from activating its own library, the image must
already have the pinned packages on R's default path,
for example in the site library. The house rule applies here as
well. Changing one value in the committed baseline file
by more than the tolerance turns the job red at the
baseline expectation. Deleting or renaming the
`test-baseline-*.R` file turns it red at the 'no baseline
test ran' check. Breaking a `RUN` line in the
`Dockerfile` turns it red at the build. Against the toy
compendium, outside a container, we ran the first two. We
also ran a baseline file whose guard found no data and
exited early. Each run of the script exited with status
1, and the unbroken run exited with 0. The image build
and the job as a whole were not run for this chapter.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## With zzcollab

The command `zzc verify` runs the same composition in two
tiers. The default *coherence* tier requires no rebuild.
It checks that the captured artifacts agree with each
other and that the R version in the lockfile matches
those in the `Dockerfile` and the project's state record.
It also checks that the backend is unambiguous and that
the raw data still match their recorded checksums. `zzc verify --full` rebuilds the
image and runs the test suite inside it. It stamps L3
into the project's state record only when the image
rebuilt, the tests passed, and at least one
`inst/tinytest/test-baseline*.R` file exists and is named
in the test log. The log names a file even when its guard
exits early with no tests, so `ci/run-tests.R`, which
counts results, is the stricter check. The stamp is
removed when `zzcollab` regenerates the Dockerfile or
when a later `--full` run falls short of L3. A change made
outside the tool, such as `renv::snapshot()` or an edited
script, leaves it in place, so a stamp older than the
last such change is stale. In regulated work the stamp is
not a validation record: it carries no signer, no stated
meaning of a signature, and no quality review.
:::

But what, precisely, should be compared? Verification
compares **computational outputs**, such as the row count
of a derived dataset, a fitted coefficient, or a
bootstrap bound, and *not* the rendered PDF or HTML. The
reason is that a rendered document is not a
deterministic function of the analysis. As @sec-literate
discussed, a PDF embeds the time of its creation and the
identifiers of the fonts the rendering machine happened to
have. Two renders of an unchanged analysis, minutes apart,
produce PDFs whose bytes differ, even though every number
in them is identical. Comparing PDFs would therefore
report a difference on every render and catch nothing real.
Comparing the estimates themselves, within a tolerance,
reports a difference exactly when a number changed by more
than floating-point noise, which is what we want to
detect. A hash is the right instrument for a file whose
bytes should not change, such as a raw data extract (the
next section). It is the wrong one for an estimate, whose
last binary digit can move under a different BLAS without
the analysis changing. There exist techniques to normalize
a document's embedded timestamps, by setting a fixed
`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, and to fix its build path. With enough
care a byte-identical PDF is attainable. But the more
general practice is to verify the computational outputs
directly and leave the document to the render gate.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

The three gates do not reach L3; only the verify job
can, by running a baseline test in a rebuilt image. This
chapter ran the gate logic and the test script, but not
the image build or the job as a whole. A green verify run
older than the last change to the lockfile, the
Dockerfile, or the code is stale, not an L3 claim. The
gates alone say nothing about whether the raw data
changed; the checksum manifest of the next section does.
In regulated work, an L3 claim is also not a validation
record (@sec-testing). Nor is a hosted run a lasting
record: GitHub deletes workflow logs and artifacts after
90 days by default, a period an organization can
change within limits
[@githubretention]. A log or artifact that supports a
claim must therefore be downloaded and kept with the
records it supports, for as long as they are kept.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: trusting an old green run

A compendium's verify job last passed three months ago.
Last week its `renv.lock` was updated to pin a new
package version, and CI has not run since. Is the old
green run still an honest L3 claim? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The run showed that a specific, now-superseded
environment reproduced the baseline, not that the
environment as it currently stands does. Because the
lockfile changed after the last successful verification
run, the claim is stale: the thing the run tested no
longer exists. The honest statement is that the compendium
was L3 as of the old lockfile and is unverified now. This
is why an L3 claim should name the commit at which the
verify job passed.
:::
:::

## Data integrity: the checksum manifest

We now turn to an input that sits outside everything the
lockfile and the container pin: the raw data itself. A
container fixes the software that reads the data, and a
lockfile fixes the packages. However, neither notices if
the data file on disk is silently altered between the
analysis and its re-execution (a row edited, a value
corrected, a column recoded). An altered input produces a
changed result with no error and no warning.

The guard is a **checksum manifest**, a small file,
conventionally `data-manifest.sha256`, that records the
SHA-256 checksum of each raw data file. Verification reads
the manifest, recomputes the checksum of each file as it
now stands, and reports a mismatch. Because any change to
a file's bytes changes its checksum, a silently altered
input is caught the next time verification runs.

To illustrate, consider a small synthetic example. We
write a tiny data file to disk, record its checksum,
write the same values again from a different kind of R
object, write a third copy with a single value altered,
and hash each file. The checksum is computed from the
file's bytes, not from the R object in memory. The point
to observe is that a one-cell change, a shift of a
single outcome from 11.1 to 11.2, produces a completely
different digest, so the alteration cannot pass
unnoticed.


::: {#tbl-integrity .cell tbl-cap='A single altered value changes the digest of a data file. The three CSV files are hashed by their bytes on disk. The second holds the same values as the first, written from a plain data frame rather than a tibble, and its digest matches. The third differs in exactly one cell, and its SHA-256 digest differs from the first character, so a checksum manifest detects the change.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(digest)
library(knitr)

cohort <- tibble(
  id      = 1:5,
  arm     = c('treatment', 'placebo', 'treatment',
              'placebo', 'treatment'),
  outcome = c(12.4, 9.8, 11.1, 10.3, 13.0)
)

hash_csv <- function(x) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = '.csv')
  write.csv(x, path, row.names = FALSE)
  digest(file = path, algo = 'sha256')
}

altered <- cohort
altered$outcome[3] <- 11.2

digests <- c(hash_csv(cohort),
             hash_csv(as.data.frame(cohort)),
             hash_csv(altered))

manifest <- tibble(
  file = c('cohort.csv (baseline)',
           'same values, from a data.frame',
           'one cell altered'),
  digest_first16 = substr(digests, 1, 16),
  matches_baseline = ifelse(digests == digests[1],
                            'yes', 'no')
)

kable(
  manifest,
  col.names = c('File', 'SHA-256 (first 16 chars)',
                'Matches baseline'),
  align = 'llc'
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|File                           |SHA-256 (first 16 chars) | Matches baseline |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------|:----------------:|
|cohort.csv (baseline)          |cc03e329ae1b1114         |       yes        |
|same values, from a data.frame |cc03e329ae1b1114         |       yes        |
|one cell altered               |632857fa64a59ad4         |        no        |


:::
:::


The altered file's digest differs from the first
character, although the files differ in a single cell.
That sensitivity to any change is what makes a checksum a
reliable integrity guard. Suppose a verification run
recomputes these digests and finds the third where it
expected the first. It has then caught an altered input,
and has done so without needing to know what the correct
value was, only that it has changed since the manifest
was recorded. The second row shows why the file, and not
the object, is what gets hashed. Hashing the tibble and
the data frame themselves with `digest()` would serialize
each object, class attributes included, and give two
different digests for identical values: here
`digest(cohort) == digest(as.data.frame(cohort))` is
FALSE.
The bytes on disk carry only the values.

A manifest line pairs a digest with a path, in the format
`shasum -a 256` writes and `shasum -a 256 -c` checks. For
this book's raw extract it reads:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
raw_path <- '../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
cat(digest(file = raw_path, algo = 'sha256'), '  ',
    'analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv', '\n', sep = '')
#> aec0973593e41aa0186ca57d44949a369323a71d9e21fcc25d6cc025b134aea7  analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv
```
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## How continuous integration adapts to the archetype

Continuous integration adapts its gates to the archetype;
@tbl-archetype-weight in @sec-compendium is the reference.
Of the three gates of this chapter, `R CMD check` and the
dependency-manifest gate are universal, run by every
archetype. The latter, however, runs in an
archetype-conditional form. It is the strict
`DESCRIPTION`-inclusion check for an R package, and the
weaker
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$ inclusion for
a compendium, as the section on the three gates
established; `ci/dependency-gate.R` implements only the
weaker form. The render gate is the conditional one. It is present
wherever a report exists, and absent from an
**R-package archetype**, which has none.

The case most worth stating here is the
**simulation archetype**, which raises a distinct concern
of cost. A full run can take hours or days. The idiomatic
arrangement therefore runs a *reduced* pipeline under CI:
a handful of iterations with a fixed seed, enough to
confirm the pipeline executes and the outputs have the
right shape. The full pipeline runs elsewhere, on a
cluster or a scheduled job, and is verified against a
baseline separately. The seeding discipline of
@sec-testing is what makes the reduced run meaningful. A
fixed seed makes even a short run reproducible, so CI
checks reproducibility rather than merely execution. A
workflow that configures itself from the files present
(@sec-ci-other-forges) can infer the archetype, but the
analyst's contribution is still to ensure that the
archetype and its gates are matched.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: when a package does need the render gate

An R-package archetype is said to have no report, so no
render gate. Under what condition does the render gate
apply to a package archetype after all, and what does it
render in that case?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The render gate applies whenever the package ships a
vignette, which is itself a rendered document. The gate
re-renders `vignettes/intro.Rmd` (or whichever vignette
files exist) on every push. It confirms that the
vignette's code still runs against the restored library,
exactly the check a manuscript's report receives. Only a
package with
neither a report nor a vignette has nothing for
the render gate to do.
:::
:::

## Independent external verification

The checking we have described so far is the author's own,
run on the author's forge against the author's baseline. It
is necessary and it is not sufficient. An author who has
misunderstood their own reproducibility can build a CI
pipeline that faithfully confirms the misunderstanding.
The complement is verification from outside the project
entirely, by someone with no stake in its passing.

The most developed such scheme is CODECHECK, described by
Nust and Eglen [@nust2021codecheck]. In it an independent
codechecker re-executes an analysis during peer review,
on their own machine, and issues a certificate recording
what was run and what was reproduced. The value of the
exercise lies exactly in its independence. The
codechecker carries none of the author's undeclared
state; this is the same property that makes a CI runner
effective, here held by a person instead of a virtual
machine. In a parallel development, major computing
venues have formalized artifact review and badging. Under
it, a submission's computational artifacts are evaluated
and, if they reproduce, marked with a badge on the
published paper [@acm2020]. Stodden and colleagues have
documented the persistence of the reproducibility
problem. They have also documented the effectiveness,
and limits, of journal policies that attempt to compel
deposition and checking [@stodden2018]. The ten rules,
for their part, ask for automated steps and public access
to scripts, runs, and results, which is what makes
independent re-execution possible [@sandve2013].

These schemes add no lockfile and no container, only a
second, independent execution of the analysis.
Continuous integration is a
machine that is not yours, and independent verification
is a person who is not you. Both
catch the reproducibility failures that the author's own
generous machine had hidden, at the last responsible
moment before a result enters the scientific record.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what independence adds beyond CI

An author's CI pipeline passes every gate, including
verification against a baseline. Why might a CODECHECK
reviewer still find something CI did not, given that both
are described as 'a machine, or a person, that is not
yours'?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

CI is configured by the author, so it tests what the
author thought to test, against a baseline the author
recorded, in an environment the author specified. If the
author misunderstood what the analysis was supposed to
produce, or recorded a baseline after a bug had already
entered it, CI will faithfully and indefinitely confirm
the misunderstanding. A codechecker reads the paper and
forms an independent judgment of what the analysis should
produce. The codechecker then checks the artifacts against
that judgment rather than against the author's own
configuration, which is a check CI structurally cannot
perform on itself.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the machinery concrete, consider a plausible
sequence of events in a cohort-study compendium, of the
kind that recurs in practice.

The analyst is refining a model and, mid-session, reaches
for a package that computes robust standard errors,
`sandwich`. They install it interactively with
`install.packages()`, and add `library(sandwich)` to
`analysis/scripts/02_model.R`, which the report sources.
They obtain the result they wanted, and commit. On their
own machine everything runs: the package is installed,
the script loads it, the report renders, the numbers
appear. The compendium looks, to its author, finished.

The push triggers CI, and the fresh runner tells a
different story, though not at the gate a reader might
expect. The runner checks out the committed files and
restores the pinned library from `renv.lock`. This
lockfile was never updated, because the interactive
install was never snapshotted. Gate 1, `R CMD check`,
passes. It is not at fault: the script lives in
`analysis/`, which the build excludes, so the check never
reads it. Gate 2, the dependency-manifest gate, reads
`analysis/` and goes red. It names `sandwich` as a
package the code uses and the lockfile does not pin. Had
that gate been absent, gate 3 would have failed the same
run from the other direction. The report sources the
script, the script calls `library(sandwich)`, and the
restored library has no such package, so the render stops
at that chunk. Either way, CI has found on a clean
machine precisely the undeclared state the author's
machine supplied silently. Had the workflow run only
`R CMD check`, as many compendium workflows do, the build
would have been green.

The fix is not to weaken the check but to repair the
capture. The analyst records the new package in the
lockfile by snapshotting the environment, commits the
updated `renv.lock`, and pushes again. This time the
runner restores a library that contains the package. The
dependency gate passes, the report renders, and the gates
go green. The `verify` job then rebuilds the image from
the new lockfile and runs the baseline test. This is
where the analyst learns whether the change moved a
recorded result, such as a confidence limit. If it did,
the baseline is re-recorded deliberately, in a commit
that says why, not loosened until it passes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

In the worked example, `R CMD check` passes even though
`sandwich` is in fact unpinned. Why does this gate miss
the defect that the dependency-manifest gate catches,
and is that a flaw in `R CMD check`?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It is not a flaw; it is a scope limit stated earlier in
the chapter. `R CMD check` runs on the package `R CMD
build` produces, and `.Rbuildignore` excludes
`analysis/`, so the check never parses, runs, or scans the
script that calls `library(sandwich)`. The gate is doing
what it is specified to do, checking the package skin.
The defect lives one directory outside that skin, which
is why a compendium needs a second gate that does read
`analysis/`.
:::
:::

## Debugging a failed reproduction

The worked example above is the easy case: CI catches the
defect the same day, on the same commit that introduced it.
The harder case arrives later. A compendium that rendered
cleanly in March fails in October, when a reviewer clones
it, a collaborator resumes it, or the author themselves
reruns it for a revision. Nothing in this section is
generic R debugging, which is out of scope for this book.
It is a diagnostic sequence specific to one question: it
worked before, and it does not now, so what changed?

The first move is to read the failing step's log on its
own terms. Identify which of the three gates reported
red: `R CMD check`, the dependency manifest, or the
render. Then read what it printed, not just that it
failed. The WARNING text or the `stop()` message usually
names the missing package or the broken chunk directly,
and often that line alone settles the question.

The second move is to reproduce that exact step locally,
from a session with the same restored library CI used,
and not as is convenient to invoke by hand ('Where CI
bugs hide', above). This is preferable to re-running the
whole render and hoping the same failure reappears in a
more informative form.

The third move asks whether the code changed, or whether
something outside the code changed under it. Consider a
pipeline that reruns the same pinned commit weeks apart
and gets a different answer. It did not fail because of
anything in a diff, and the fix is to compare
environments, not history. `sessionInfo()`
(@sec-dependencies and the glossary) is the cheapest
comparison. It is run in the working environment and the
failing one, and the two are diffed by eye for an R
version, platform, or package version that moved.
`renv::status()` goes further, comparing the project
library with the lockfile and reporting packages that are
missing or installed at a different version. When the
suspicion lands on the lockfile itself,
`git diff <good-sha> <bad-sha> -- renv.lock` shows
exactly which package or version entries changed between
two commits. This narrows 'something in the environment
changed' to the one or two packages responsible.

The fourth move applies only if the analysis is a
`targets` pipeline (@sec-pipelines). The diagnostic then
moves into the dependency graph. `tar_outdated()` lists
which targets the pipeline considers stale and therefore
due to rerun, and `tar_visnetwork()` draws the same
information as a graph. The analyst can then see where in
the chain of targets the invalidation begins. This holds
provided the pipeline's metadata store, `_targets/`,
survived the problem. On a fresh CI runner it is absent
unless it was committed or the workflow restores it, and
a pipeline run there without it rebuilds every target.

The last move, when the log and the environment have not
explained the failure, is to localize it in time.
Suppose the history between the last known-good state and
the present failure holds more than a handful of commits.
Reading each one is then slower than letting git find the
boundary. `git bisect` does this by binary search. Told
one commit that is good and one that is bad, it checks
out the midpoint and asks for a verdict, halving the
remaining range at each step.

```bash
git bisect start <bad-commit> <good-commit>
git bisect run Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'
git bisect reset
```

`git bisect run` automates the verdict. It checks out each
candidate commit and runs the given command, taking a
nonzero exit status as 'bad' and zero as 'good'. It
continues until a single first-bad commit remains. We
verified the mechanism on a disposable four-commit toy
repository, under git 2.55.0. The first commit
established a check that passed. The second, an
unrelated-looking refactor, silently changed a value the
check depended on, and two further commits added only
comments. We marked the fourth commit bad and the first
good with `git bisect start`, then ran
`git bisect run Rscript check.R`. It
tested the midpoint, found it still bad, and tested the
commit below that. It then named the second commit as the
first bad one, in two bisection steps rather than three
linear checks. The command handed to `bisect run` can be
the render gate or a baseline test from @sec-testing,
which lets the search run unattended across dozens of
commits. Bisection can blame a commit only if the
environment at each checkout is otherwise identical,
which is why the environment comparison comes first.

None of these five moves is a substitute for the others,
and the order runs from cheapest to most expensive.
Reading the log is the cheapest move, and the log often
names the cause.
Reproducing the step locally confirms it. Session-info
and lockfile comparisons then settle whether the defect
is in the code or in the environment around it.
`targets` diagnostics apply only when a pipeline is
involved. Bisection is the most expensive move, and it is
reserved for a failure that the first four have not
explained.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: bisecting an environment problem

A pipeline's render step fails on a Tuesday rerun of a commit
that rendered cleanly the previous Friday. The commit has not
changed. Why will `git bisect` be useless here, and what
should be compared instead?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

`git bisect` localizes a failure to a commit by checking out
different revisions and testing each one, which only works
when the thing that changed is in the history it walks. Here
the commit is fixed and identical on both days, so bisection
has nothing to vary and nothing to find; every checkout it
tries is the same code. The defect lies outside the commit,
most likely in the restored environment: an unpinned
dependency that resolved to a different version between
Friday and Tuesday, or a base image whose tag moved. The
right comparison is `sessionInfo()` or
`renv::status()` run on both days. If the lockfile
itself is suspect, it is a diff of `renv.lock` against the
copy captured on Friday. It is not a bisection across
commits that never changed.
:::
:::

## Demonstrating a gate on the cohort compendium

The logic that runs on a CI runner also runs, in
miniature, on this book's own cohort compendium, without
any CI infrastructure at all. Below, a short script
mirrors the dependency-manifest gate of the earlier
section. It finds every package `R/cohort.R` actually
uses, compares that list against what this compendium
currently declares as pinned, and reports whether the
gate passes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
used <- unique(renv::dependencies('../../R/cohort.R')$Package)
#> Finding R package dependencies ... Done!
locked <- names(renv::lockfile_read('../../renv.lock')$Packages)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))

gate_check <- function(missing) {
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop('Used but not pinned in renv.lock: ', toString(missing))
  }
  'gate passed'
}

missing_now <- setdiff(used, c(locked, base_pkgs))
cat('Packages R/cohort.R uses:', toString(used), '\n')
#> Packages R/cohort.R uses: parallel, stats, survival, tibble, utils, withr
cat('Missing from the pinned set:',
    if (length(missing_now)) toString(missing_now) else '(none)', '\n')
#> Missing from the pinned set: (none)
cat('Result:', gate_check(missing_now), '\n')
#> Result: gate passed
```
:::




The gate passes. `R/cohort.R` uses
`parallel`, `stats`, `survival`, `tibble`, `utils`, and `withr`, and each is either pinned in `renv.lock` or part of base R.
The house rule of this book applies
here as well: a gate shown only to pass has not been
shown to work. We therefore run the same script against a
`used` list with the chapter's own running example of an
unpinned dependency added. It shows what a real CI log
would print the moment someone adds `library(sandwich)`
to a cohort script without snapshotting it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
used_broken <- c(used, 'sandwich')
missing_broken <- setdiff(used_broken, c(locked, base_pkgs))
result <- tryCatch(gate_check(missing_broken),
                   error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat('Missing from the pinned set:', toString(missing_broken), '\n')
#> Missing from the pinned set: sandwich
cat('Result:', result, '\n')
#> Result: Used but not pinned in renv.lock: sandwich
```
:::


The injected package is named, and the step would stop
with a nonzero exit status in real CI. The failure points
at the undeclared dependency, which is what the
dependency-manifest gate is for. Restoring `used` to its
real value (dropping the injected `sandwich`) returns the
gate to green, as reverting the offending commit would on
a real runner.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Collaborating with an LLM

A large language model is a capable assistant for CI work,
which is heavy on boilerplate YAML. It is also a
hazardous one, because CI failures are subtle and a
plausible-looking workflow can still be wrong. We give
three prompt patterns, each with what to watch for and
what the analyst must independently verify.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data through
prompts with public generative AI tools, which it glosses as
third-party tools, as a breach of the data use certification.
It treats a model trained on such data as a data derivative,
to be shared only with other approved users and not kept
after the project closes [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.

An agent also acts, so confine it to a branch and keep merges,
pushes, and deposits for yourself (@sec-llm-delegate).
:::


CI touches data in ways that are easy to miss. A CI log
that prints rows of a failing render or test is a derived
output in the sense of the rule above, so a log excerpt is
pasted only after those rows are removed. For CI work the
structure to describe is the workflow file and the error
message.

**Prompt.** 'Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `R
CMD check` on my compendium inside the `rocker/tidyverse`
container and restores packages from `renv.lock`.'

*Watch for.* A workflow that restores the library in one
step and runs the check in another without ensuring the
restored library reaches the check subprocess. As we saw,
adjusting the library path in one step does not carry to
the next, and `R CMD check` runs in a child process that
sees only the library path it is handed. Check for the
naive two-step form, which passes only when every
dependency happens to be in the base image. Watch also
for `error_on = 'error'`, a dependency
step that reports without failing, and
`continue-on-error: true`. Each of these leaves a gate
that cannot go red. Remember, too, that `R CMD check`
alone never looks at `analysis/`.

*Verification.* Do not trust the workflow because it is
syntactically valid. Confirm it fails correctly by
introducing a deliberate gap: import a specialized
package absent from the base image, do not restore it,
and check that the build goes red. A CI check that has
never been seen to fail has not been shown to work.
Seeing means reading the run log yourself: a coding
agent's report that 'CI is green' is a claim about the
run, not an observation of it.

An agent asked to make a failing build pass can reach
green by the patterns this triple lists, adding
`continue-on-error: true` or loosening `error_on`, and
the change arrives as an ordinary commit. Treat
`.github/workflows/` as a protected path and read every
line of any diff that touches it before it merges. CI is
also where embedded instructions matter most. An agent
that reads a log, an issue, or a downloaded file can be
steered by text planted in it, and in CI it may run with
the repository's secrets. Grant its jobs the least
privilege of @sec-ci-secrets, and keep pushes and
merges with the analyst (@sec-llm-delegate).

**Prompt.** 'Add a verification step that checks my analysis
reproduces, by hashing the output and comparing it to a
saved value.'

*Watch for.* A step that hashes the rendered PDF or HTML.
The report is the most visible output and the wrong
thing to hash, because its bytes carry timestamps and
font identifiers and change on every render.

*Verification.* Insist that the target is a computational
output. Estimates should be compared with a committed
baseline within a stated tolerance, in a
`test-baseline-*.R` file, while hashes are kept for files
whose bytes should not change. Confirm by rendering the
report twice without changing the analysis: the report's
own bytes should differ while the baseline test still
passes. If the model's chosen target changes between the
two renders, it is the wrong target.

**Prompt.** 'My compendium is a simulation study that takes
six hours to run. Write CI for it.'

*Watch for.* A workflow that attempts the full run on every
push, which will time out or consume the CI budget, or one
that runs so few iterations that it no longer tests
anything meaningful.

*Verification.* Confirm the workflow runs a reduced,
fixed-seed pipeline under CI and defers the full run
elsewhere. Check that the reduced run is seeded so that
its short output is itself reproducible. Verify that the
number of iterations in the reduced run is large enough to
exercise the code paths that matter, not merely one.

*A better prompt.* 'My compendium's simulation runs
`<B>` replicates in about six hours; `R/` holds the
functions and `inst/tinytest/` the tests. Write a GitHub
Actions workflow that, on each push, runs the tests and
a fixed-seed run of `<b>` replicates within 20 minutes,
pins each action by commit SHA, and never sets
`continue-on-error`. Say where the full run should
happen instead, and what deliberate change I should
make to confirm that each step can fail.'

In each case a syntactically valid workflow is the easy
part to check. The semantics, what the check actually
proves and whether it can fail for the right reason, are
what the analyst must verify and cannot delegate.

## Exercise 2

**`R CMD check`** catches a defect in the package skin as
code. One example is a function in `R/` calling a package
that is used but not declared in `DESCRIPTION` (a
WARNING, so the gate must fail on warnings). Others are a
syntax error in a file under `R/` that nothing currently
calls, or a documented argument that no longer exists.
The render gate would not see it if the report does not
touch that function. The manifest gate checks
declarations rather than whether the code loads.
The same defects under `analysis/` are invisible to
`R CMD check`, which never sees that directory.

**The render gate** catches a defect that appears only when
the document is built. Examples are a chunk that fails on
a clean machine because it read an uncommitted file, a
figure whose code errors, or a cross-reference to a label
that no longer exists. `R CMD check` never renders, so it
sees none of this.

**The dependency-manifest gate** catches drift between the
code and the manifests: a package used in a script under
`analysis/` and missing from `renv.lock`, which
`R CMD check` never sees. In its strict form, for the
package archetype, it also catches a package declared in
`DESCRIPTION` and missing from `renv.lock`, a check that
`ci/dependency-gate.R` does not make. The code may load
and the
document may render perfectly on a machine where the
package happens to be installed, so neither other gate
fires.

**A failure none of the three catches:** a change in the
*data*. A raw extract silently replaced with a corrected
version leaves the code valid, the document renderable,
and the manifests consistent. Meanwhile every number in
the report changes. All three gates pass. The
**data-integrity gate** addresses it, by hashing the
inputs and derived outputs and comparing against a
recorded manifest.

The **verification gate** addresses the adjacent case in
which the code changes a result without any of the three
noticing. It does so by comparing computed outputs
against recorded baselines.
:::
